items.answer: Empirical study is a usability-testing stage in interactive system development, performed after code testing, that systematically tests a fully implemented system with end users through a controlled experiment to collect and analyze data for assessing overall usability.
An experiment is the designed and executed part of an empirical study that collects and compares objective data to answer a research question and measure the usability of an implemented interface.
An independent variable is a variable whose values are assigned and controlled; these values are called levels and are used to design an experiment.
A level is a value assigned to an independent variable or factor in an experiment.
A test condition is a combination of factor levels that is used to design an experiment.

Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user: the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

questions.question: In an experiment, why should the selected participants be chosen carefully?
options: to simplify the whole user group
to recruit the whole user group
to define the whole user group
to represent the whole user group
questions.explanation: The participant subset stands for the full user group, so conclusions remain valid and reliable only when the subset represents that group. A subset does not define the group; the user profile does.

questions.question: When is a homogeneous participant subset acceptable in an experiment?
options: when the participants are from a homogeneous user group
when the system is for a homogeneous user group
when the system is for a heterogeneous user group
when the experiment is for a homogeneous user group
questions.explanation: A homogeneous subset can support conclusions for a system aimed at a homogeneous group, but it cannot reliably support conclusions for a heterogeneous user group. The acceptable case depends on the system's target group, not merely on the experiment or the participants' background.

questions.question: What should be used first when choosing participants for an experiment?
options: a software stack with well-defined characteristics
a device set with well-defined characteristics
a user profile with well-defined characteristics
a task list with well-defined characteristics
questions.explanation: Participants are selected on the basis of a user profile, which specifies relevant user characteristics. User characteristics such as age or computer-use frequency belong to that profile, not to the tasks, devices, or software being evaluated.

data.text: Experiment participants are a sample of all potential users, so their representative selection is what makes conclusions valid. A user profile gives the well-defined characteristics used to define and choose those participants. A homogeneous group can be used when the system targets that group, but broader heterogeneous groups require profile characteristics such as age and computer-use frequency.
points: Experiment participants are a sample of potential users; without representativeness, conclusions are not valid or reliable.
A homogeneous user group is acceptable only when the system is for that group, not for heterogeneous user groups.
A user profile is a set of well-defined characteristics used to define the user and select experiment participants.
Experiment participant selection using user profiles must consider age and computer-use frequency, which can affect typing behavior and speed.

questions.question: Why is a participant set below the commonly used range treated as a problem in a controlled empirical experiment?
options: because tasks may not be representative and may not cover the interface's full use
because data may mostly be subjective and may not support interface claims
because task order may add practice noise and may hide interface effects
because conclusions may not be reliable and may change if participants are added
questions.explanation: A participant set that is too small may not support reliable conclusions, and those conclusions may change when the set is increased. The other options concern task choice, data type, or task-order effects, not the participant-count issue.

questions.question: In a controlled experiment evaluating an interface, what kind of task-performance data are usually the main basis for conclusions?
options: objective data collected while users perform tasks
subjective ratings collected while users perform tasks
narrative reports collected while users perform tasks
expert judgments collected while users perform tasks
questions.explanation: Controlled interface experiments usually rely on objective task-performance data collected from users. Subjective ratings, narrative reports, and expert judgments are not the usual main basis described for this kind of experiment.

questions.question: Why might a controlled interface experiment use a small subset of the tasks its system supports?
options: because a practice effect can make repeated task performance noisy
because a between-subjects design divides the task set among participant subsets
because time and practicality limit the available task set to a careful choice
because a Latin square design shifts the task order for each participant
questions.explanation: Only a small subset of an interface's tasks can often be used because of time and practical limits, so the subset must be chosen carefully. The other options describe design or analysis choices, not the reason for limiting the task set.

questions.question: What makes a task set representative for an interface that will be used in practice?
options: a short, simple subset of tasks that experienced users can finish very quickly
a small, well-defined subset of tasks that deployed users most commonly use
a broad, detailed subset of tasks that exercises rare system features
a random, mixed subset of tasks that comes from user reports
questions.explanation: A representative task set is a small, well-defined subset of tasks that potential users most frequently or commonly use when the interface is deployed. Rare features, ease for experienced users, or random user reports do not make the set representative.

questions.question: Why is a random piece of text not a representative task for comparing typing interfaces?
options: because text strings are chosen to cover interface activity and skills
because older people may have different typing behavior than teenagers
because regular computer users may type faster than infrequent computer users
because a within-subject design can add practice noise to repeated typing performance
questions.explanation: A random text passage is not representative because representative typing tasks use text strings selected to indirectly encompass interface activity and users' typing skills. The other options concern user differences or experimental design, not what makes the text task representative.

data.text: A controlled empirical study of an XR interface relies on objective task-performance data, so the participant count and the selected tasks shape whether conclusions about the interface are reliable. The participant number is generally kept between 12 and 25, and the small tested task subset should represent tasks potential users commonly use in practice. These choices together help the experiment avoid unreliable conclusions about the interface.
points: Controlled empirical experiments usually use 12 to 25 participants, though more can be used; fewer may be unreliable.
Controlled interface experiments collect mostly objective task-performance data to draw conclusions about the interface.
The tested task subset should be a small, carefully chosen representative set of tasks potential users use most in practice.

questions.question: In an experimental interface study, what does a within-subject design require of participants?
options: Every participant does the tasks for one test condition
Every participant does the tasks for all test conditions
Every participant does the tasks for alternate test conditions
Every participant does the tasks for a share of test conditions
questions.explanation: A within-subject, or repeated-measures, design has every participant perform the tasks associated with all test conditions. A between-subjects design instead divides the conditions among different participants.

questions.question: Why might a between-subjects design be chosen even though a within-subject design is easier to manage?
options: Limited participant or resource availability may make using the same numbered task sequence for each participant necessary
Limited participant or resource availability may make dividing the tasks among different participant groups necessary
Limited participant or resource availability may make repeating the same tasks for each participant necessary
Limited participant or resource availability may make assigning a single task to each participant necessary
questions.explanation: A within-subject design is easier to manage, but limited participants or resources can make a between-subjects arrangement necessary, in which tasks are split among different participant groups. Repeating tasks or task orders for each participant, or assigning a single task to each participant, is not the reason stated.

questions.question: Why can a practice effect confound the analysis of a within-subject study?
options: Performance gains may come from practice rather than the interface
Performance gains may come from chance rather than the interface
Performance gains may come from the interface rather than practice
Performance gains may come from the task list rather than practice
questions.explanation: Practice effect is an improvement in task performance caused by repeated practice, so it can add noise by making it unclear whether gains come from the interface or from practice. Reversing the cause or blaming chance or the task list does not describe this confound.

questions.question: How does a Latin square design reduce the practice effect in a within-subject study?
options: By shifting a numbered task sequence for each successive participant
By repeating the same task sequence for each successive participant
By randomizing the task sequence for each successive participant
By reversing the task sequence for each successive participant
questions.explanation: A Latin square design systematically varies the task sequence, for example by shifting a numbered sequence one position for each successive participant, so the practice effect is spread across conditions. Randomization can also reduce practice effects, but a Latin square is specifically a systematic variation.

data.text: Task assignment in an XR user experiment contrasts within-subject and between-subjects designs, depending on participant and resource availability. Within-subject designs are easier to manage, but repeated practice can confound the data because performance gains may reflect practice rather than the interface. Randomizing or systematically varying task sequences, such as using a Latin square, is intended to statistically nullify that practice effect.
points: Task assignment can be within-subject, where every participant does all test conditions, or between-subjects, where conditions are divided among participants.
Within-subject designs are easier to manage, but participant or resource limits may force a between-subjects design.
A practice effect confounds within-subject analysis by adding noise, since gains may reflect practice rather than the interface.
Within-subject task sequences can be randomized or systematically varied, such as with Latin squares, to statistically nullify the practice effect.

questions.question: In empirical interface studies, how do the collected data and the intended conclusions differ in scope?
options: The data come from a sample, while the conclusions concern the measuring equipment
The data come from a sample, while the conclusions concern the experimental tasks
The data come from a sample, while the conclusions concern a larger population
The data come from a sample, while the conclusions concern the selected participants
questions.explanation: Empirical interface studies collect data from a limited set of users, but the conclusions of interest are about the wider user population. Treating the tested participants as the only people of interest misses the intended generalization.

questions.question: What does a statistically significant difference tell a researcher about an observed data difference?
options: It is due to chance and reflects the tested conditions
It is large in absolute value and reflects the tested conditions
It is not due to chance and reflects the tested conditions
It is not due to chance and reflects participant preferences
questions.explanation: A significance test is used to decide whether an observed difference is likely to be reliable rather than a chance outcome. Statistical significance concerns the role of chance and the tested conditions, not merely the size of the difference.

questions.question: What is required before a researcher can conclude that one text-entry interface is faster?
options: A larger absolute value for the faster group's mean
A statistically significant difference between the means
A non-significant difference between the means
A repeated test with the same participants
questions.explanation: A higher mean speed alone may occur by chance, so the difference between the group means must be statistically significant before one interface can be judged faster. Absolute mean size or repeating the test with the same participants is not the stated requirement.

data.text: Data analysis in system implementation checks whether empirical results are reliable before design claims are made. Interface studies use user samples to support population-level claims, so an observed advantage may only reflect chance. A statistical significance test therefore distinguishes chance differences from condition-related differences, and text-entry comparisons require a significant relative difference between group mean speeds.
points: In system implementation, stage 4, data analysis, tests empirical data for statistical significance before drawing conclusions about design efficacy.
Empirical interface studies collect data from a sample of users, but conclusions concern a larger population.
Straightforward conclusions may be chance, so a statistical significance test checks whether a difference is due to chance or conditions.
Comparing text-entry interfaces requires a statistically significant relative difference between mean text-entry speeds, not absolute values or a higher mean.

questions.question: Which non-parametric significance test is indicated for a within-subject design with a nominal or categorical scale of measurement and one factor having two levels?
options: Mann-Whitney U test
Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Chi-square test
McNemar's test
questions.explanation: For a nominal or categorical outcome with one factor at two levels, the non-parametric test is chi-square for a between-subject design and McNemar's test for a within-subject design. Wilcoxon signed-rank and Mann-Whitney U are used for one-factor two-level designs without the nominal or categorical condition, and Mann-Whitney U is a between-subject test.

questions.question: Which non-parametric test can also be used for a between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels?
options: Mann-Whitney U test
Friedman test
Kruskal-Wallis test
Wilcoxon signed-rank test
questions.explanation: A between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels can use the non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test. The Friedman test is for within-subject designs, while Mann-Whitney U and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests apply to one-factor two-level designs.

questions.question: In a statistical significance test, what does a lower p-value indicate?
options: The observed difference is less likely to have been obtained by chance
The observed data are more likely to have been obtained by chance
The observed effect is less likely to have been obtained by chance
The observed data are less likely to have been obtained by chance
questions.explanation: A p-value is the probability of obtaining the data by chance, so a lower p-value means the data are less likely to have arisen by chance. It describes the probability of obtaining the data, not merely the observed difference or effect.

questions.question: What determines the method for performing a statistical significance test?
options: The task sequence in the experiment and the nature of the input data
The number of participants in the experiment and the nature of the input data
The design of the experiment and the nature of the input data
The number of conditions in the experiment and the nature of the input data
questions.explanation: The appropriate significance test depends on the experiment's design and the nature of the input data. Participant count, task sequence, and condition count are not the factors given as determining the test method.

data.text: Choosing a statistical test to check whether differences in empirical XR experiment data are significant depends on the experiment design and input data. Statistical significance tests are divided into parametric and non-parametric tests. The choice then differs for two-level designs and for designs with more levels or factors, since different between-subject and within-subject tests apply in each case.
points: The statistical significance test used depends on the experiment design and the nature of the input data.
Significance-test results can include group-means difference, p-value, T value, degrees of freedom, and significance; lower p-values mean less likely.
Statistical significance tests fall into two groups: parametric tests and non-parametric tests.
For one-factor two-level designs, choose between- or within-subject tests according to measurement scale and design type.
For more levels or factors, choose between-subject one-way or factorial ANOVA or within-subject repeated-measures ANOVA.

questions.question: Why does using a homogeneous participant sample limit the user group to whom conclusions about an interface can be generalized?
questions.reference_answer: A sample must be representative of the whole user group for its conclusions to be valid or reliable. A homogeneous group has members with the same or similar age, educational, socio-economic, and cultural backgrounds, so it can represent a homogeneous target group. It does not represent a heterogeneous group, so conclusions from such a sample are not reliable for that broader group.

questions.question: Why does choosing a random piece of text weaken conclusions about the overall usability of a typing interface?
questions.reference_answer: An empirical study can use only a small subset of all supported tasks, so that subset must be chosen carefully. A random piece of text is not a representative task, because representative tasks are commonly used strings chosen by metrics and measures that indirectly encompass the whole interface and users' typing skills. Data from a non-representative task may not support a reliable conclusion about overall usability.

questions.question: How does a Latin square design reduce the practice effect in a within-subject experiment?
questions.reference_answer: In a within-subject design, repeated practice can improve performance and confound the analysis. A Latin square design systematically varies the task sequence, for example by shifting it one position for each successive participant. These variations are supposed to nullify the practice effect, so gains are less likely to be mistaken for an interface effect.

questions.question: Why is a higher mean text-entry speed by itself insufficient for concluding that one text-entry interface is better?
questions.reference_answer: The analysis compares the relative difference between the mean text-entry speeds of the two groups rather than the absolute values. A higher mean alone may be due to chance, because an observed difference may appear even when the conditions do not cause it. A statistical significance test is needed to show that the difference is not due to chance; only a statistically significant difference supports concluding that one design is better in speed or efficiency.
